This observable reveals the detailed structure of QCD radiation from heavy quarks, allowing for a distinction between perturbative and non-perturbative effects in charm-quark showers. We then discuss measurements of the angular differences between three different axis definitions inside the jets. The three definitions offer different sensitivity to wide-angle soft radiation and systematically probe the radiation pattern from charm quarks. The final measurement regards jet angularities, which characterize the weighted angular distribution of the jet constituents. These powerful observables probe the parton shower, with sensitivity to parton-mass and Casimir-factor related effects that can be tuned by adjusting the importance of wide-angle radiation.

papers.title: Entanglement distillation, nonlocal magic, and state sharing in an isospectral non-Hermitian bipartite model
papers.summary: An invertible nonunitary similarity deformation leaves a two-qubit Hamiltonian's spectrum unchanged while varying a selected normalized right eigenstate in the fixed physical inner product. We embed this state in a two-parameter maximally correlated family that includes local dephasing and noisy circuit preparation. Hashing and a matching diagonal relative-entropy bound give the exact distillable entanglement and the PPT comparison distances at every finite tensor power. Correlated PPT catalysts cannot improve the Bell-pair distillation rate. The optimized CHSH value is \(2\sqrt{1+t^2}\): every state with nonzero coherence violates CHSH, while complete dephasing is separable. A calibrated finite-sample bound and two equal-fidelity preparations clarify which noise parameters determine the rate. For pure inputs, the binomial Schmidt spectrum gives logarithmic collectively optimized nonlocal magic with vanishing density, despite a positive entanglement density and extensive pairwise-frame magic. Fixed Clifford decoding gives six- and eight-copy CCZ concentration probabilities \(P_6=\frac12(1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ})\) and \(P_8=1-2^{-\mathcal M_γ}\). The same family permits explicit swapping recursions, symmetry-resolved entanglement, and a comparison of qubit stabilizer and fermionic Gaussian resources. These calculations keep the relevant operation classes separate when comparing many-copy limits.

papers.title: Local topology hallucinations in universal machine-learned interatomic potentials
papers.summary: Predicting metastable states with universal machine-learned interatomic potentials requires that they preserve the minima and saddles of the reference potential-energy surface. Here we identify local topology hallucination, in which distinct model minima relax into the same reference basin. This failure arises from mode-selective curvature-sign errors shared by MACE, CHGNet and M3GNet. Curvature signs predicted by two of the three models agreed with density-functional calculations in 55 of 57 positive but only 5 of 56 negative cases. In LiGe$_2$S, two MACE minima connected by a verified saddle relaxed into one density-functional basin. Reference relaxation likewise returned nine of ten selected model minima to their reference basins. A directional test with two displaced reference calculations rejected 9 of 12 prospectively tested model instabilities. Model agreement alone therefore cannot establish that predicted minima are distinct metastable states.

papers.title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
papers.summary: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.

papers.title: A conditional quadrature method of moments for populations of oblate spheroidal particles
papers.summary: Non-spherical particle populations are encountered in numerous industrial processes, where particle size, shape, and velocity jointly influence transport, breakage, and classification dynamics. The resulting coupled distributions of geometric and kinematic particle properties evolve within a high-dimensional phase space whose accurate representation remains a significant challenge. We present a conditional quadrature method of moments (CQMOM) for oblate spheroidal particles described by a five-dimensional phase space that includes their size, aspect ratio, and velocity. The dimensionality of the problem is reduced by assuming that the particles continuously adopt their drag-maximizing orientation. In the solution algorithm, the resulting conditional quadrature representation of the particle phase space is combined with a Strang splitting of the continuous and discontinuous mathematical operators governing the moment transport. We verify this CQMOM framework against Monte Carlo simulations of the same particle model for representative test cases of increasing complexity, including drag, breakage, recoil, and attrition, at different Stokes numbers. With two nodes per coordinate, the particle number, the mean size, and the mean aspect ratio agree with the Monte Carlo solution within its statistical uncertainty, and the velocity statistics to within 7 %. Time-step and quadrature resolution studies identify the conditional velocity quadrature as the main source of the remaining deviations, for which we discuss potential remedies. Overall, the results demonstrate that the conditional quadrature representation preserves the geometric-kinematic correlations of the particle population in a five-dimensional phase space, at a cost more than 60 times lower than that of a single Monte Carlo realization.

papers.title: Differentiable Exact Learning
papers.summary: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.

papers.title: Lost in the Hallway: Benchmarking Persistent Spatial Memory Across Revisits
papers.summary: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.

papers.title: Ice and mirrors
papers.summary: Given a mirror pair of smooth affine principal upper cluster varieties admitting reddening sequences, we show that homological mirror symmetry for principal cluster varieties -- assumed compatible with certain cluster structures -- descends under freezing. This allows us to induct on the following class. A skew-symmetrizable matrix is peelable if, by mutations and removing sinks or sources, it can be reduced to the empty matrix; it is sub-peelable if it is a principal submatrix of a peelable matrix. We establish homological mirror symmetry for full rank upper cluster varieties whose mutable matrix is sub-peelable. We show sub-peelability for the Fock--Goncharov SL(n) quiver for any compact surface with nonempty boundary, all of whose boundaries have markings. Consequently, we establish homological mirror symmetry between the moduli of decorated SL(n) local systems and the corresponding pinned PGL(n) spaces. The results were obtained using ChatGPT Astra.

papers.title: Input-to-State Stability in Distributed Adaptive Identification of Nonlinear Systems without Input Sharing
papers.summary: This paper studies continuous-time distributed adaptive identification of unknown nonlinear systems over directed communication networks without requiring source or neighboring inputs to be shared. Each sensing node reconstructs the source state while adapting local estimates of the unknown linear and nonlinear dynamics using only locally available information and neighboring state estimates. A network-level error representation is derived to characterize the interaction among the communication topology, observer dynamics, parameter uncertainty, and nonlinear mismatch. Norm-based, structured Lyapunov, and robust LMI conditions are established to guarantee that the resulting coupling operator is Hurwitz. Unlike the corresponding discrete-time formulation, the proposed continuous-time adaptive laws do not require normalization. A Lyapunov analysis establishes boundedness of the adaptive parameters and asymptotic convergence of the estimation and source-tracking errors in the unperturbed case. Input-to-state stability is further established under bounded predictor mismatch and source disturbances. Numerical studies over star, cyclic, and path topologies support the theoretical results and demonstrate approximately linear computational scaling with the number of sensing nodes.

papers.title: Renormalization group study of critical behavior of $O(m)$ model with cubic anisotropy and extended defects: two-loop approximation
papers.summary: We study the impact of quenched extended defects correlated in $ε_d$ dimensions and randomly distributed in the remaining $d - ε_d$ dimensions on the critical properties of a $d$-dimensional $O(m)$-symmetric system with cubic anisotropy. Exploiting the field-theoretic renormalization-group approach within the minimal subtraction scheme, we compute the two-loop renormalization-group functions. Applying resummation techniques to analyze the asymptotic series, we estimate the marginal values of $ε_d$ above which disorder becomes relevant for the physically important cases $m = 2$ and $m = 3$ in $d = 3$. We report numerical values of the critical exponents for the disorder-induced universality classes.

papers.title: Quantum Networks with Realistic Photonic Memories
papers.summary: Ensemble based photonic memories paired with photon pair sources are the essential ingredient for many quantum networking protocols. Most protocols and theoretical analyses focus on networks of identical nodes, however, realistic networks consist of nodes that may vary from device to device. We investigate a network of non-identical memories and develop mitigation strategies for the variation in performance. We find that by strategically distributing the memories among the nodes and individually adapting the emission probabilities based on the memory efficiency the effect of the variance on fidelity and duration can to a large extend be mitigated. Generally, our analysis shows the importance of accounting and compensating for device variations to avoid deteriorating the performance. Lastly, we also link our results to memories where efficiency decays as a function of storage duration. Here, we show that our approach provides a visible improvement for networks with non-identical and decaying memories.

papers.title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
papers.summary: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.
papers.comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience (IEEE CSR 2026)

papers.title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
papers.summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

papers.title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility
papers.summary: A useful memory need not resemble the question it helps answer. Jetriever ranks each stored memory by Jev's decision score for its usefulness to the current question, replacing similarity search with full-pool utility scoring. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, it places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases; matched BM25 and MiniLM controls reach 1.6% and 0.0% when indexing user turns. A 20-question comparison separates finding evidence from ranking it: Jev and Qwen3.5 9B each find 90% of gold exchanges by rank 50, while Laya finds 30%; at rank one, Jev reaches 85% and Qwen3.5 9B 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever's four-dimension score is 55.4%, against 44.3% for ReFind on the same questions. Jev retrieval costs USD 0.00834 per InMind question and USD 0.03103 per MAB question on average. These results show the value of world knowledge, scores that rank decisive memories first, and affordable full-pool scoring.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables. Project repository: https://github.com/imlrz/Jetriever

papers.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
papers.summary: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

papers.title: Energy spectrum of trions in semiconductors
papers.summary: Energy levels of trions in a bulk semiconductor crystal are calculated by two different numerical methods. On the one hand, we construct the finite-element solution of the Schrödinger equation in the total angular momentum representation. On the other hand, we use the Gaussian expansion method (GEM), applied to each of the three Faddeev components of the wave function. The results for the total angular momenta $J=0$ and $J=1$ of the trion were obtained for a wide range of the hole-to-electron mass ratios covering most existing semiconductor compounds. The dependencies of the energies on the mass ratio for trions in a bulk crystal qualitatively agree with the results for a simplified model of a trion in a 1D quantum wire, for which the three-body energies can be calculated with arbitrary precision as well as easily approximated using Born-Oppenheimer potential-energy curves. A comparison of our results with data from other publicly available three-body codes as well as with the energies of well-known atomic counterparts, in particular, with vibrational energy levels of the molecular hydrogen ion, shows a good agreement and confirms the accuracy of the numerical data. We found that GEM significantly improves the precision of the obtained trion energies compared to previous calculations. Our calculations demonstrate that, for most semiconductor compounds, only one trion state with zero total angular momentum exists.

papers.title: Sharp High-Dimensional Gaussian Approximations over Rectangles without Covariance Restrictions
papers.summary: We study how well a sum of $n$ independent random vectors with $p$ coordinates can be approximated by a Gaussian vector with the same mean and covariance. We measure the error over rectangles, so the bounds apply to maxima and simultaneous confidence regions. The coordinates may be arbitrarily dependent, even exactly linearly dependent, and the bounds do not deteriorate as the covariance matrix becomes singular. After standardizing the coordinate variances, bounded or sub-exponential coordinates give the $n^{-1/2}$ sample-size rate up to logarithmic factors, with the size or tail bounds held fixed. The main upper bounds retain the Gaussian expected maximum, improving the rates when the coordinates are strongly dependent. Fourth-moment refinements give further improvements when large observations contribute little to individual coordinate variances. If we instead impose a fixed moment bound of order $q>4$ on the largest absolute coordinate, together with a coordinate fourth-moment bound, the rate becomes $n^{-1/2+1/q}$ up to logarithmic factors. At $q=4$, the slower $n^{-1/4}$ rate is unavoidable, confirming our earlier conjecture. We also allow the bounds on observation size to grow with $n$. Lower-bound examples show that the dependence on sample size, observation size, and Gaussian width is sharp up to logarithmic factors in the regimes studied, and in several regimes the upper and lower bounds match including the logarithmic terms.
papers.comment: 107 pages. Supplemental Material (28 pages) and archived Lean verification: https://github.com/VC2015/rectangle-clt-singular

papers.title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework
papers.summary: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.
papers.journal: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management 2026

papers.title: Event-Triggered Visual Perception for Real-Time Harvest Outcome Estimation in Mechanical Blueberry Harvesting
papers.summary: Mechanical blueberry harvesting requires a balance between removing ripe fruit and avoiding premature removal of unripe berries that could remain on the bush for a later harvest. However, operators generally lack real-time information about the maturity composition of the fruit being collected. This study develops an event-triggered machine-vision system that measures the maturity of harvested blueberries directly on the harvester. When a filled crate is moved by the machine, an RGB image is automatically captured and analysed using a three-class detector that identifies ripe, semi-ripe, and unripe berries. The system operates locally on the existing CPU-only industrial computer and therefore requires neither continuous image processing nor dedicated GPU hardware. During field testing, 79 crate images containing 48,634 visible blueberries in manually verified reference annotations were evaluated. The vision system estimated an overall ripe-fruit fraction of 90.22%, compared with 90.97% determined manually. Per-image ripe-fruit estimates showed a mean absolute error of 0.935 percentage points and a Pearson correlation of r=0.967. Maturity estimates remained similar between the two sides of the harvester for which the light conditions varied despite poorer absolute counting performance under direct sunlight. All field events were processed within the available 14 s per-side crate interval. The proposed approach provides a practical means of quantifying one component of harvest selectivity while the machine is operating. Such information could support operator decision-making and, when combined with measurements of fruit recovery and losses, contribute to future feedback-based control of mechanical harvesting.

papers.title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
papers.summary: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.
papers.comment: To appear at NeurIPS '26. Code available at https://github.com/jrgan/VSI

papers.title: A proof of the Reinhardt conjecture
papers.summary: We prove the Reinhardt conjecture: among centrally symmetric convex disks in the plane, the smoothed regular octagon has the least optimal lattice packing density, and equality holds precisely for its nonsingular affine images. The proof combines explicit bounds on the number of control arcs, local cost inequalities and rigorous finite verification of the remaining switching types.
papers.comment: The purpose of this paper is to show that the conjecture can be resolved. The present proof is long, and the author hopes that further work will lead to a shorter and more beautiful proof

papers.title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
papers.summary: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

papers.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: Observed Sensitivities to the Wide-Separation, Cold, Sub-Jupiter Exoplanet Population
papers.summary: We present a sensitivity analysis of three recent JWST direct imaging programs (GO-4050, GO-5835, and SURVEY-6005) designed to build a demographic study of sub-Jupiter mass ($0.1 - 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$) exoplanets in nearby young associations and moving groups. We find that these programs are sensitive to sub-Saturn to Jupiter mass exoplanets with effective temperature (T$_\mathrm{eff}$) as low as $\lesssim 250$ K, already at $\sim 2$ arcsec. A comparison with the SHINE survey confirms that the improvements in mass sensitivity provided by JWST high-contrast imaging surveys outpace current ground observation for masses $\lesssim 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$ and separations between $\sim20-500$ au, opening up a novel parameter space to explore. Overall, this analysis provides a robust framework for interpreting future exoplanet detections. By correlating photometrically derived properties (e.g. mass, $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and separation) with theoretical model predictions, we show how the access to potentially low detectable masses (sub-Saturn to Jupiter) strongly depends on the expected atmospheric chemistry of the exoplanet population.
papers.comment: 40 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Accepted for publication at AJ

papers.title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
papers.summary: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

papers.title: A spherical body in plasma simulated with adaptive mesh and algorithm refinement
papers.summary: An absorbing sphere in a weakly ionized plasma is the oldest kinetic problem of probe theory. It presents key difficulties in plasma simulation: disparate velocity scales, orbital motion, phase-space regions that no characteristic of the plasma reaches, a boundary set by a kinetic flux balance, and collisions that qualitatively change the answer. We use this problem to demonstrate the Plasma Adaptive Mesh and Algorithm Refinement (PAMAR) framework introduced in a companion paper. Electrons and ions have separate solvers on their own adaptive $(r,v,μ)$ octrees, or on reduced phase spaces at the angular-moment level (Fokker-Planck and two-stream models), coupled through a radial Poisson field solver. Two exact references, a method of characteristics for the collisionless problem and integration along the orbits for elastic scattering, audit the solvers. We compute the current-voltage characteristic of the probe on both electron and ion branches, and the profiles of the potential and of the moments of both species agree with the exact solution. Far from the sphere, the potential follows the Coulomb law in neither limit: it falls as $r^{-2}$ without collisions and as $r^{-1}$ only beyond the ion mean free path. With elastic electron scattering, the kinetic solver follows the exact dependence of the collected current on the mean free path, from free flight toward diffusion, to 1 percent. Finally, we demonstrate the ion model selection cell by cell, using a fluid model coupled to the kinetic solver, with the interface set by the pressure anisotropy; with charge exchange, a sensor of ion trapping is also needed. According to exact solutions, the ion anisotropy extends to several probe radii, much farther than the electron loss cone.

papers.title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
papers.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

papers.title: Windowed Singularity Subtraction for the Spectral Integral Method
papers.summary: In 2004, the spectral integral method (SIM) was proposed to solve TM$_z$ scattering by homogeneous two-dimensional dielectric objects and perfect electrical conductors with smooth boundaries. Its error decreases exponentially as the number of boundary points increases linearly. Plasmonic resonances, however, require TE$_z$ polarization and permittivities with a negative real part. The extension of SIM to this case shows that the original global singularity subtraction suffers catastrophic cancellation, with a round-off floor that grows exponentially with the attenuation accumulated across the object. To resolve this issue, this work introduces a windowed singularity subtraction that limits this cancellation amplification to an exponential factor that the user can set independently of the object size, provided the window is adequately resolved. Numerical results verify the accuracy of the proposed method.

papers.title: Controlling Mode-Locking in Liquid Light
papers.summary: Mode-locking is the process by which the phases of many cavity modes organize collectively into a stationary state. In lasers, mode-locking originates from the interplay of gain, loss, dispersion and nonlinearities, most commonly resulting in the emission of short pulses. However, pulse formation is prevented when the gain recovery is fast enough to suppress amplitude fluctuations. Mode-locking then produces an extended state of nearly constant intensity, whose dynamics is governed by the phase. Yet, a general framework for designing the phase of such extended photonic states remains lacking. Here we introduce a hydrodynamic approach to designing extended photonic states, in which the phase dynamics are understood and controlled as a flow of liquid-like light. The intensity, clamped by fast gain, plays the role of a constant density, the instantaneous frequency that of a flow velocity, and the programmable radio-frequency modulation applied to the laser acts as a potential landscape that controls the flow. We derive analytical solutions connecting the applied modulation to the instantaneous frequency and hence to the spectrum emitted by the laser. We further provide experimental evidence for the liquid light shaping framework by measuring the frequency comb spectra emitted by a fast-gain semiconductor laser around \SI{1.6}{\micro\m} under the control of a programmed modulation, and comparing them to the ones predicted by the analytical solution. The hydrodynamic picture of mode-locking provides a predictive design principle for frequency combs, pointing toward a programmable synthesizer of light, and establishes fast-gain lasers as an accessible, electrically driven platform for nonequilibrium fluids of light.

papers.title: Multi-bubble blowup for the energy supercritical Schrödinger equation
papers.summary: This article establishes the existence of finite time multi-bubble Type II blowup solutions for the focusing energy supercritical nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Given integers $K\geq 2$ and $L\geq 2$, a positive integer exponent $p$, and a dimension $d>d_\ast(p,K,L)$, we construct solutions concentrating at any prescribed $K$ distinct points $\{x_j\}_{j=1}^K\subset\mathbb R^d$, with the asymptotic form \begin{equation*} ψ(t,x)=λ^{\frac1p}(t)\sum_{j=1}^K Q\big(λ(t)(x-x_j)\big)+ζ^\ast(x)+o_{\dot H^σ}(1),\qquad t\to0, \end{equation*} where $λ(t)=t^{-\frac12-ν}$, $ν=-\frac12-\frac{L}{λ_+}$, $s_c=\frac d2-\frac1p$, and $s_c<σ<s_c+\frac{4ν}{1+2ν}$. Here $Q$ is the positive radial stationary profile, $λ_+$ is the slow characteristic exponent in its asymptotic expansion at infinity and $ζ^\ast$ is the limiting radiation determined by the outer profile. The proof combines a matched asymptotic construction of a finite order approximate solution with high order energy estimates and a compactness argument. The key ingredients are the elimination of the self-similar oscillatory branch through a quantized choice of blowup rate and the quantitative control of the combined algebraic tails of the translated ground state potentials.

papers.title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
papers.summary: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

papers.title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
papers.summary: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.

papers.title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
papers.summary: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.

papers.title: Expertise capture in workplace AI
papers.summary: AI assistants are becoming part of how knowledge workers think and perform, accumulating the prompts, exemplars, memory and interaction histories that encode a worker's professional judgment. This infrastructure typically runs under employer or platform control. We name the resulting process expertise capture, the absorption of worker-applied knowledge and judgment into AI resources under organizational control. We develop a framework of contribution forms, technical residences and transformation families, and show that how far a contribution can be attributed, separated and revoked depends on where it resides and how it has been transformed, properties fixed by system design long before any dispute arises. When a worker departs, the organization retains a capability shaped by their judgment while the worker loses access to it, and the asymmetry compounds as contributions move from inspectable artifacts into derivatives, learned components and successor systems. We outline three measures, write-time provenance, extraction of separable contributions and an executable exit procedure, that make an agreed allocation technically performable, and make explicit what cannot be separated at all.

papers.title: Experimental simulation of a Hilbert-space inner-product change
papers.summary: We simulate an effective change in a single qubit's inner product (IP) by implementing the channel $\mathcal{F}^η$ on a superconducting quantum processor. Whereas previous experiments simulated parity-time (PT)-symmetric dynamics with a fixed IP, this experiment implements the IP-change channel itself for metrics associated with PT-symmetric systems. Building on an earlier adversarial verification approach, we derive a process-fidelity threshold that rules out mixtures of qubit unitary operations with random discarding of runs. We test the channel for 40 metrics using a single qutrit and a two-qubit Stinespring dilation. The measured fidelities exceed the threshold in 24 of 40 qutrit instances after readout error mitigation, compared with 16 of 40 unmitigated two-qubit instances. Without mitigation, 14 of 40 qutrit instances pass. These results demonstrate a direct simulation of an effective Hilbert-space IP change and its verification against a specified adversarial class, while showing the importance of readout treatment in comparing the encodings.

papers.title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
papers.summary: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.

papers.title: Plenitude of ideal correlations explains quantum theory
papers.summary: We show that the Hilbert-space formalism and the Born rule of quantum theory are singled out by the following principle: every correlation that is possible in a theory in which every observable admits an ideal measurement is physically realizable. An ideal measurement is one that yields the same outcome when repeated and does not disturb any compatible observable.

papers.title: Robust Action Clusters and Cascades in Opinion Dynamics with Heterogeneous Action Thresholds
papers.summary: We study the preservation and propagation of public actions in networks whose agents hold continuous private opinions. Agents update their opinions from their neighbors' observed actions and express them through action rules whose thresholds differ across agents. We characterize groups of agents that preserve a given common action regardless of the outsiders' actions. We call such a group, paired with that action, a robust action cluster. We show that a group is a robust action cluster for that action if and only if each member places enough of its influence weight on the group, where the required influence depends on the member's own action rule. We further give a sufficient condition under which an agent outside the cluster permanently adopts the cluster's action, and we iterate it to obtain a cascade of agents that are guaranteed to adopt that action. Finally, numerical examples show that replacing heterogeneous thresholds by their mean can change both the propagation of an action and the presence of robust action clusters.

papers.title: Localization transition in a spin chain with an exact Fock-space tree
papers.summary: Many-body localization is often pictured as Anderson localization on the graph of many-body configurations. Strongly correlated disorder and a dense net of loops, however, make this graph hard to analyze. We introduce a local disordered spin-1 chain in which a single domain wall explores an exact binary tree of configurations. Random fields create strongly correlated disorder on this tree, as in generic interacting systems, while the absence of loops keeps the problem tractable. We rigorously bound the spreading of the domain wall at strong disorder, and efficient numerics on exponentially large trees indicate a localization transition at finite disorder strength.

papers.title: Quantum Optimization Algorithm for Pinching-Antenna Activation with Max-Min Fairness
papers.summary: In this letter, we propose a training-free quantum approximate optimization algorithm with a linear-ramp schedule (LR-QAOA) for antenna activation in pinching-antenna systems (PASS). Since all active pinching antennas (PAs) share one feed and split its power, maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the weakest user becomes a combinatorial max-min problem that must be re-solved whenever the users move. We formulate the problem as a two-local Ising Hamiltonian with one qubit per PA and no penalty terms, employing a weightedsum surrogate to prioritize weaker users. Instead of training the circuit with a classical optimizer, the proposed LR-QAOA method tunes its parameters via a linear ramp; the measured patterns are ranked by the exact max-min objective, and the best ones are refined with a short local search using the same number of evaluated patterns. Monte Carlo simulations show that the proposed LR-QAOA method outperforms greedy activation, projection-guided activation, and semidefinite relaxation-based classical baseline methods when all methods test the same number of PA on/off patterns. Experiments on real IBM Quantum hardware further show that the execution time remains nearly constant as the number of PAs grows, whereas exhaustive search grows exponentially. However, gate noise in the NISQ era restricts near-optimal hardware solutions to small numbers of antennas only.

papers.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
papers.summary: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

papers.title: [CLS] and [EOS] Tokens are not Enough for CLIP-based Class-Incremental Learning
papers.summary: Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to empower models to continuously acquire new knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. With the advent of vision-language models like CLIP, leveraging their cross-modal alignment capabilities to address CIL challenges has emerged as a dominant paradigm. Existing methods leverage CLIP's global representations (i.e., the visual [CLS] token and the textual [EOS] token) for cross-modal alignment. While achieving effective classification, they overlook the rich patch-level visual features and token-level textual semantics inherent in CLIP. For example, the [CLS] token aggregates local information to capture the general concept of "cat", while the patch-level details retain specific localized features essential for recognition, such as the tail, fur, and face. We propose PACE (PAtch-token Cross-modal Enhancement) to uncover the long-neglected local representations within CLIP. First, based on the global representations like [CLS] token and [EOS] token, we identify the top-k most crucial visual patches and textual tokens. Subsequently, to better utilize the extracted key local features, we design a cross-modal fusion module. This module leverages local textual semantics to refine visual representations, while augmenting textual semantics with local visual features. As the fusion module is shared across all tasks, directly fine-tuning it on new tasks would interfere with the knowledge learned from previous tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting. To alleviate this, we employ a projection-based update strategy to effectively preserve the critical parameter space of previous tasks during the adaptation to new tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple CIL benchmarks.
papers.comment: Accepted to TMM. Code is available at: https://github.com/LAMDA-CL/PACE

papers.title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
papers.summary: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

papers.title: Power Line Detection in Point Clouds with Point-SAM and RANSAC
papers.summary: This article deals with the problem of detecting the position of power lines in airborne laser scanning point clouds. We address both the problem of segmenting power lines from background like ground and vegetation and of identifying individual lines. For segmentation we compare a rule-based approach with one based on transfer learning (Point-SAM). For individual line detection, we derive the mathematical formulas for RANSAC applied to 3D catenaries and compare it with a non-parametric method (TriplClust). All methods are evaluated on a newly created dataset "PowLiDFR", which we make publicly available. The samples have been taken from the French project LiDAR HD and cover a variety of terrain layouts and point cloud resolutions. On this dataset, an unsupervised transfer learning outperformed a mere rule-based segmentation, and for individual power line detection, RANSAC was better in following the shape of catenaries than the non-parametric algorithm.

papers.title: A First Look at Astrometric Outer Companions to Super-Earths and Sub-Neptunes using Gaia DR2 and DR3
papers.summary: Massive outer companions (OCs) are believed to promote, inhibit, or otherwise regulate the formation and composition of inner small planets (ISPs) both in the solar system and in exoplanetary systems. To assess how, we leverage calibrated absolute astrometry from Gaia DR2-DR3 of 7,321 FGKM dwarfs and present measurements of the relative occurrence rate of OCs in systems hosting known ISPs (i.e. P(OC$|$ISP)/P(OC)), including systems with inner super-Earths only, inner sub-Neptunes only, and across a range of spectral types and stellar metallicities. We search for OCs in pairs of planet and reference stellar samples using the orbital fitting framework Octofitter and characterize the occurrence of OCs in mass--semi-major axis space under a Bayesian hierarchical model. We find an excess of OCs in systems with ISPs ($1.77\pm0.49$), independently supporting results from radial velocity surveys for the first time using astrometry. We recover similar excesses in both super-Earth (SE; $2.02\pm0.52$) and sub-Neptune systems (SN; $1.97\pm0.50$), highlighting that OCs do not inhibit the formation of ISPs, regardless of planet type. We argue that the consistency across SE and SN systems supports ex-situ formation, wherein ISPs form rapidly at larger separations prior to OCs opening disk gaps, thus providing evidence of Type I migration of SEs and SNs. We also evaluate how these results vary across stellar mass and metallicity, finding that M dwarfs exhibit an OC excess that is $1.41\pm0.78\times$ stronger than that around FGK dwarfs, and not finding a significant dependence on metallicity, contrary to previous radial velocity surveys.

papers.title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
papers.summary: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.
papers.comment: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026. The first two authors contributed equally. 41 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/MinchanJeong/NestedLoRA-VMC

papers.title: Kinetic Monte Carlo modeling of ammonium formate NH$_4^+$HCOO$^-$ and ammonium cyanate NH$_4^+$OCN$^-$ in interstellar ices
papers.summary: JWST observations have revealed evidence for NH$_4^+$ in the ices of the Chamaeleon I dark molecular cloud, with HCOO$^-$ and OCN$^-$ likely counter ions. Laboratory experiments have demonstrated that ammonium formate and ammonium cyanate can form through acid-base reactions involving NH$_3$ at cryogenic temperatures. The formation of these two ammonium salts are simulated to investigate their formation in dark-cloud ices and assess their sensitivity to uncertainties in the chemical reaction network, including the recently considered HOCO-mediated pathway for CO$_2$ formation, as well as variations in the cosmic-ray ionization rate, cloud collapse timescale and density, and elemental depletion. Our modeling framework consists of microscopic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) simulations of grain-surface chemistry augmented by UCLCHEM gas-phase and physical cloud evolution simulations. The microscopic KMC method provides for explicit simulation of the location, movement and reaction of ice species, making it particularly well-suited to model acid-base chemistry of NH$_4^+$-salt formation, occurring within the ice mantle over extended timescales. The simulations produce the canonical ice-evolution sequence, with an initially H$_2$O-rich ice followed by a layer dominated by CO and CO$_2$. Salt production is dominated by NH$_4^+$HCOO$^-$, which is found to form predominantly during the H$_2$O-rich stage as its production is limited by the availability of NH$_3$. NH$_4^+$OCN$^-$ is found to form later at the interface between the H$_2$O- and CO-rich ice when the formation of its precursor acid HNCO is enabled. Despite the variations explored, the total NH$_4^+$ abundance, particularly relative to H$_2$O, remains remarkably robust and consistent with the observed abundance. Depending on the variation, a redistribution between counterions HCOO$^-$ and OCN$^-$ is observed.

papers.title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
papers.summary: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.
papers.comment: 4 pages, 3 tables. Data, code and protocols: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24286137

papers.title: On the toric Bando--Kasue--Nakajima conjecture
papers.summary: The conjecture of Bando, Kasue, and Nakajima asserts that every simply connected Ricci-flat $4$-manifold that is asymptotically locally Euclidean (ALE), that is, asymptotic at infinity to a flat cone $\mathbb{R}^4/Γ$, is hyperkähler for one of its orientations. A toric ALE instanton is a Ricci-flat ALE $4$-manifold with an effective isometric action of the $2$-torus; such a manifold is simply connected. We prove the conjecture for the toric ALE instantons whose group at infinity $Γ$ is conjugate in $\mathrm O(4)$ to a subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$: each of them is a multi-Eguchi--Hanson metric with collinear centres. In particular, the conjecture holds for toric ALE instantons with $|Γ|\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$. The proof uses a closed formula for toric gravitational instantons, which expresses the metric through Hankel determinants of a positive measure on the fixed points of the torus action. With it, the problem becomes a question about lattice points in a parallelogram determined by the end.

papers.title: Geometry of squeezed states. The phase-space metric, relative vacua and cosmology
papers.summary: Geometry enters quantum theory in two places. The space of quantum states carries a symplectic form, which generates unitary evolution, and a metric, which governs uncertainties and transition probabilities. The classical phase space acquires a metric of its own when a vacuum is chosen: quantizing a linear system amounts to choosing a compatible complex structure, equivalently a compatible metric $g$. We take this second metric as the primary object and show that it plays, on phase space, the role that the quantum metric plays on the space of states: fluctuations of linear observables are $g$-norms of Hamiltonian vector fields, and along coherent states $g/2\hbar$ \emph{is} the quantum metric. Squeezed states then have a simple description. A squeezed vacuum is the vacuum of another metric, and squeezing is a property of a pair of metrics, a relative vacuum, whose invariants are the eigenvalues $e^{\pm2r_i}$ of $L=g_0^{-1}g$. We work out the harmonic oscillator in detail, including why a rotated squeezed state no longer minimizes the product of the displayed uncertainties. Quadratic evolution deforms the metric, and only the part of the generator that is self-adjoint with respect to the reference changes the $r_i$, at a rate we give exactly. For fields, a vacuum is unitarily implementable relative to a reference exactly when it lies at finite distance from it in the space of vacua. For a massless field in de Sitter space we revisit the two canonical charts compared by Grain and Vennin: relative to the reference of the standard squeezing formalism the Bunch--Davies state has $\sinh r_k=1/(2|kη|)$, and relative to the vacuum that a radiation era beginning at time $η$ would select it has $\sinh r_k=1/(2k^2η^2)$. The second comparison squeezes twice as fast and is unitarily implementable; the first is not.

papers.title: Randomization protects the average, not the trial: chance covariate imbalance and a calibration of balance $P$ values at the design stage
papers.summary: Randomization makes the unadjusted treatment-effect estimate unbiased over the allocations a scheme could produce, although it does not balance any single trial. Chance imbalances on strongly prognostic baseline variables directly threaten the validity and regulatory credibility of trial results, yet what design-stage balance $P$ values imply for bias and error rates is seldom stated. We review evidence on chance covariate imbalance and derive that link under a linear model with one normal prognostic covariate, with simulation checks. Given the realized allocation, the unadjusted estimate is biased by $β$ times the difference in covariate means; in standard-error units the bias is $ρZ_{\mathrm{bal}}$, where $ρ$ is the covariate-outcome correlation and $Z_{\mathrm{bal}}$ the balance z-statistic, so it does not shrink as trials grow. Pre-specified ANCOVA removes this bias, change scores reverse it, and non-collapsibility attenuates odds and hazard ratios even under perfect balance. A worst-balance threshold of $P = 1/e$ marks where the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound reaches 1; under complete randomization the worst of $k$ independent balance $P$ values falls below it with probability $1-(1-1/e)^k$, 0.99 for $k=10$. Any balance $P$ value $\geq 0.317$ keeps the two-sided conditional type I error of the unadjusted test at or below 5% for every $ρ$; at $1/e$ the one-sided error in the favoured direction is at most 4.1%, against 13-33% at $P = 0.05$. Design-stage balance scores should be benchmarked against complete randomization, weighted by external prognostic strength, and reported alongside allocation predictability and a pre-specified covariate-adjusted analysis plan.
papers.comment: 36 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; includes Appendix S1 (derivations, 9 tables, 12 figures). Python code to reproduce every number and figure is in the ancillary files and at doi:10.5281/zenodo.24210820

papers.title: Instant Folded Strings: Fractal Decay and ANEC Saturation
papers.summary: Instant Folded Strings (IFSs) present a puzzle. On the one hand, they appear to be an intrinsic part of string theory: they are fundamental closed strings nucleated classically in backgrounds in which the string coupling grows toward the future, and they have been argued to play an important role in black-hole interiors and cosmology. On the other hand, their energy-momentum tensor violates the Averaged Null Energy Condition (ANEC), placing IFSs in tension with standard causality and unitarity arguments. We show that finite string coupling resolves this tension by triggering a decay cascade that saturates the ANEC in Minkowski spacetime. The remnant of the original IFS persists indefinitely, continuously seeding a self-similar fragmentation cascade that produces infinitely many strings over its full history. In the semiclassical regime, the cascade is governed by a single Malthusian exponent, $κ_{\mathrm{IFS}}=2\sqrt{2}-2$, which controls the branching growth, pressure decay, cutoff-ANEC convergence, and anomalous non-integer dependence on the string coupling. The complete state has vanishing total energy and momentum while remaining highly excited and carrying negative integrated pressure on every finite time slice. This provides a concrete example of genuinely stringy low-energy dynamics in which microscopic null-energy consistency coexists with macroscopic negative pressure.

papers.title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models
papers.summary: Machine learning models for chemical reaction prediction are usually evaluated by endpoint accuracy, but endpoint correctness alone does not reveal how a model represents chemical transformation or why it fails. We introduce UniRxnAxis, a unified forward-retrosynthesis framework that models both tasks as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space. By aligning source states, transformed states, and encoded target endpoints, UniRxnAxis enables directional auditing of learned latent updates. This shared latent geometry allows the learned displacement (from the encoder source state $S_0$ to the decoder-facing transformed state $S_1$) to be decomposed into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual, which we call emergent steering. Our evaluation shows that emergent steering is functionally important: in retrosynthesis, it recovers most of the model's utility, remains effective under random, shuffled, and prototype controls, and directly affects which bond edits are promoted or suppressed. The residual-over-parallel ordering persists across alignment strengths, after decoder-interface calibration, against angle-matched random axes, and in a second graph-edit architecture, although its magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization. The decomposition also supports a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures, showing how reaction models can be audited beyond endpoint accuracy.

papers.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
papers.summary: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

papers.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
papers.summary: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces.
