Evaluating these claims requires distinguishing how an algorithm achieves an advantage from what is necessary for the separation and how strongly it is supported against classical alternatives. We propose a multi-label taxonomy that makes these distinctions explicit, classifying structural, interference, and coherent mechanisms while separately recording their necessity and the evidence for the classical comparison. Coherent mechanisms are further divided into memory and output, reflecting distinct restrictions on quantum information processing. A two-part entanglement-breaking test distinguishes loss of information from loss of algorithmic efficiency. The hidden subgroup problem illustrates the distinction: among the cases examined, cross-copy coherence is information-theoretically necessary only for the symmetric group. We present this as a diagnostic methodology rather than a theory of quantum advantage: for a new claim, it identifies the relevant adversary, separates the mechanisms a protocol uses from those shown to be necessary, and records the strength of the evidence and the quality of the advantage separately.

papers.title: Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning Coding for Index Assignment in Semantic Communications
papers.summary: Transmitting quantized semantic embeddings over a bit-flip channel requires a binary mapping that minimizes expected reconstruction distortion. The classical Binary Switching Algorithm (BSA) ($\mathcal{O}(K^3 \log K)$ for $K$ centroids) yields locally optimal assignments but ignores hierarchical bit significance, making it incompatible with Unequal Error Protection (UEP). We propose Recursive Spectral Graph Partitioning (RSGP), which recursively bisects the centroid affinity graph along the Fiedler eigenvector so that early bits separate semantically distant groups while later bits refine local structure. RSGP runs in $\mathcal{O}(K^3)$ with no iterative outer loop, and is the only method studied to show a systematic positive UEP gain: protecting early bits over later ones improves accuracy for RSGP, while being neutral or harmful for unstructured assignments. Experiments on the Banking77 dataset and the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) confirm that RSGP consistently matches or exceeds BSA accuracy across codebook sizes and error profiles.

papers.title: Specifying & Verifying Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
papers.summary: Building quantum computers is challenging due to the noise that affects qubits. Quantum error correction tackles noise by encoding information in quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes. These codes are often complex, increasingly found by computational search, presented in diverse formalisms with informal arguments, and hard to reason about algorithmically. Given that the rest of the quantum computing stack relies on a QEC code's properties for correct computation, we propose a formally verified foundation for QEC codes. We present QECLean, a Lean-based framework for formally specifying and verifying QEC codes. QECLean backs every claimed QEC-code property with a machine-checked proof, unifies the diverse presentations of codes in the literature through common abstractions, and makes new codes easy to specify. We present a new compositional technique, code combinators, for proving code distance analytically. Code combinators allow us to prove the distance of large codes that are out of reach for algorithmic techniques; for example, we show that IBM's $[[360, 12, \leq 24]]$ code has distance 24, which was previously only known as an upper bound. Furthermore, we show how our approach allows us to formalize and prove entire code families, such as the surface code. Our work lays the foundation required for reasoning about circuit-level implementations of codes on given architectures and for building end-to-end verified compilers for quantum computers. QECLean is available at https://github.com/Stavan-Jain/QECLean

papers.title: Shrink Responsibly: Empirical Bayes in Economics
papers.summary: Empirical researchers are often interested in the relative causal impact of individuals or institutions such as teachers, schools, hospitals, or neighborhoods. Regression-based estimates of such unit-specific parameters are often noisy; empirical Bayes (eB) methods can help isolate the signal from the estimation noise. This article provides an overview of eB methodology, showing how eB shrinkage can improve compound decisions---such as selecting individuals with the highest causal impacts---even when the working model motivating the shrinkage is misspecified. Not all analyses benefit from eB shrinkage, however, and we discuss which types of causal summaries are best estimated directly and how to do so robustly. We illustrate practical takeaways with a running analysis of public elementary and middle school value-added.

papers.title: Investigating the Benefit of Transfer Learning from the Locus Coeruleus for Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta Segmentation
papers.summary: The substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) is a small midbrain nucleus that degenerates early in Parkinson's disease (PD). T1-weighted FLASH MRI enables its visualization and may support early detection of neurodegeneration. However, manual segmentation is difficult and time-consuming, and deep learning models often suffer from the limited availability of labeled data. Transfer learning (TL) may help by adapting pre-trained models to small datasets. We investigate whether TL from a model trained on the locus coeruleus (LC), a nucleus with a similar appearance in this sequence, improves SNpc segmentation. Several TL strategies were evaluated using a 3D U-Net. With as few as 5-14 labeled subjects, TL and training from scratch achieved similar performance, reaching a Dice similarity coefficient of up to 0.77, close to reported inter-rater agreement. No TL strategy differed significantly from training from scratch, suggesting that initialization from the LC offers no significant benefit for SNpc segmentation.
papers.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027

papers.title: Immersive virtual reality in learning physics: a systematic review of opportunities and challenges
papers.summary: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) can heighten presence and enable active, embodied interaction in realistic 3D environments, which has been associated with potential benefits in physics education. This article presents a comprehensive review of IVR implementation in physics education at both school and university levels. The analysis included 34 studies indexed in Scopus and ERIC, published between 1 January 2018 and 1 June 2025. Methodologically, this review followed a preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses approach. IVR implementations for physics learning were assessed, topic-aligned activity types were summarized, and associated opportunities and challenges were documented. Findings indicate that IVR can support physics learning by providing complementary visualizations, optimizing cognitive load, enabling haptic learning, saving time, and fostering collaborative inquiry. Conversely, the most frequent potential IVR challenges include discomfort, unreliable interaction, orchestration issues, relatively high costs, and significant extraneous cognitive load.

papers.title: Low-energy states of a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain connected perpendicularly to a metallic lead
papers.summary: Recently, Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains (SSHCs) coupled to metallic leads have attracted attention. In particular Martínez {\it et al.} [Phys. Rev. Res. {\bf 8}, 043118 (2026)] studied a topological SSHC connected at one of its ends perpendicularly to a metallic lead modeled by a tight-binding chain. Here, we extend their results by incorporating the finite-size splitting of the end modes of the isolated SSHC, which are determined analytically with high accuracy. We also derive simple analytical expressions, valid in the low-energy regime, for the zero-temperature conductance through the lead and the relevant spectral densities. We find that, when the chemical potential coincides with that of the half-filled SSHC, the conductance reaches its maximum value, equal to that of the lead in the absence of the SSHC. By contrast, the conductance vanishes when the chemical potential is shifted by an amount equal to half the end-mode splitting.

papers.title: Weak lensing data beyond flexion
papers.summary: In weak lensing, shear and convergence are well studied and have provided a wealth of information about the distribution of matter in the universe. More recently, flexion -- the next term in the multipole expansion of the lensing potential, responsible for the characteristic banana-shaped distortion of lensed images -- has been shown to provide additional constraints on the mass distribution of lensing systems, particularly for galaxy clusters. Here we investigate whether weak-lensing information beyond flexion is similarly useful for lens-mass reconstruction. Using the roulette-amplitude formalism, we construct synthetic datasets for a single SIE lens and for SIE and SIS cluster lenses, with and without simulated Gaussian noise, and perform a least-squares reconstruction of the lens parameters using amplitudes truncated at third (flexion), fourth, and fifth order. As a proof of concept, we find that higher-order amplitudes do provide additional, useful information: the benefit is modest for a single lens, where flexion already constrains most parameters, but becomes substantial for cluster lenses, where the rotation and ellipticity are otherwise poorly recovered. The improvement is most pronounced in the presence of noise, where third-order reconstruction can become unreliable while higher-order amplitudes restore much of the lost accuracy. These results suggest that, as weak-lensing surveys grow in depth and precision, data beyond flexion could meaningfully improve mass reconstruction for the most complex and noisiest lensing systems, motivating further work using observational rather than synthetic data.

papers.title: Moiré Excitons in a Chern Ferromagnet
papers.summary: Recent experiments have established excitonic optical resonances as powerful probes and control knobs of moiré Chern ferromagnets. However, the microscopic nature of excitons formed on such interaction-driven, time-reversal-symmetry-broken ground states remains largely unexplored. In this paper, using a Gutzwiller plus Bethe-Salpeter equation framework, we investigate twisted bilayer MoTe2 at hole filling ν_h=1 and identify two near-infrared Chern-ferromagnet excitons (CFEs) selectively coupled to opposite circular polarizations. Strong electron-hole interactions markedly enhance their energy separation and drive a pronounced momentum-space reconstruction of the emergent X- state, beyond the quasiparticle-transition picture. We further find that this reconstruction enhances the interlayer electron-hole character of X-, giving rise to a giant quadratic Stark response. These findings reveal the nontrivial interplay between electron-electron correlations and electron-hole interactions underlying CFE formation, providing optical fingerprints of moiré Chern-ferromagnetic order and a microscopic basis for its optical control.

papers.title: Verifiable Random Sampling of Private Data Without a Trusted Single Party
papers.summary: Problem: When a party supports claims about a private dataset by disclosing a sample, auditors cannot tell whether it was drawn at random or "cherry-picked" to hide flaws in the rest of the data. Solution: The data holder commits to the hashes of every item in its dataset and registers the commitment with independent servers. Selection then waits on a decentralized randomness beacon: a network that jointly emits a fresh random value every few seconds, outside the control of the data holder and the auditors. The value emitted two beacon rounds after the commitment picks the sample. Each server returns a signed receipt, so anyone can later check that the revealed sample is exactly the one that value prescribes. Selection from the committed set stays unbiased as long as the beacon's threshold holds and one required server is honest, and a pre-agreed name, checked with the servers, stops repeated or abandoned draws. We call this protocol NoCherry. Applications: Any audit that spot-checks a private corpus: private AI benchmarks and held-out test sets, dataset quality claims, code and security audits, test-fairness review, vulnerability handling, and compliance sampling. Auditors need not trust the data holder to hand over a representative sample of the committed data, since the protocol proves it, and data holders need not expose their entire dataset.

papers.title: Fluid exchange and renewal in the left atrial appendage
papers.summary: Fluid exchange through the opening of a cavity does not uniquely determine how the cavity is washed out. We investigate this phenomenon in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a deforming side cavity of the heart, using simulations of 17 patient-specific atria with wall motion reconstructed from time-resolved computed tomography. Fluid exchange through the LAA ostium is decomposed into a component driven by LAA volume change and a component due to simultaneous bidirectional flow, with no net volume transport. Washout of a scalar initially confined to the LAA is compared with predictions from two well-mixed washout models and assessed alongside residence-time distributions. Volume-driven transport accounts for approximately 24-78% of total exchange across the simulated atria. Relative washout efficiencies are approximately 26-53% with respect to the inflow-driven washout model that assumes scalar-free inflow. A scalar-balance decomposition identifies two contributions to this discrepancy: re-ingestion of previously expelled scalar and preferential export of scalar-poor fluid. Both effects reduce the effective washout rate in every configuration. Residence-time distributions reveal coexisting distinct younger and older fluid regions, and a regional analysis of one appendage localizes the older population predominantly in its distal region. These findings show that substantial exchange across the LAA ostium coexists with prolonged distal retention. Effective renewal depends on how much fluid crosses the ostium and which fluid is exchanged.

papers.title: Heavy-quark gluon radiation in transversely flowing QCD matter: First-subeikonal corrections
papers.summary: We investigate medium-induced gluon radiation from energetic heavy quarks propagating through a finite-size QCD medium with transverse collective flow. Within the DGLV framework, we calculate the radiation spectrum at first order in opacity and to first-subeikonal accuracy, retaining finite heavy-quark and effective gluon masses. Subleading corrections to the longitudinal propagator poles generate mass-dependent modifications of both the residue denominators and formation phases. For rotationally symmetric transverse-momentum integration domains, all contributions linear in the transverse flow velocity vanish after full azimuthal integration, while a nonzero static first-subeikonal correction remains. For representative medium parameters, this correction increases the integrated fractional radiative energy loss by approximately $10$--$20\%$, depending on the quark mass, initial energy, and path length. At the differential level, transverse flow produces a dipolar angular anisotropy, enhancing radiation along the flow direction and suppressing it in the opposite direction.

papers.title: Torsional Hall Viscosity of Massive Chern Insulators: Finite Temperature and Chemical Potential
papers.summary: We study the torsional Hall viscosity $ζ_{\rm H}$ of Chern insulators at finite temperature and chemical potential. Our analysis considers the massive Dirac fermion and two deformations: a constant out-of-plane magnetic field and a momentum-dependent mass described by the single-block Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (BHZ) Hamiltonian. For the massive Dirac theory, we show that temperature and chemical potential lead to UV-finite corrections and that a chemical potential outside the bulk gap modifies $ζ_{\rm H}$ even at zero temperature. In a constant magnetic field, the response of massive Dirac fermions is dictated by the relativistic Landau-level spectrum, leading to a plateau structure at zero temperature that is smoothed at finite temperature. The jumps are proportional to the Dirac mass and inversely proportional to the squared magnetic length and the newly occupied Landau-level energy. Finally, we present a detailed study of the correction to $ζ_{\rm H}$ in the single-block BHZ continuum model due to temperature and chemical potential. For parameters relevant to (Hg,Mn)Te quantum wells, the magnitude of the jump across a mass domain wall retains its vacuum enhancement due to the BHZ deformation as long as the chemical potential lies sufficiently deep inside the gap compared with the thermal energy. Our results extend the theory of torsional Hall viscosity to experimentally relevant conditions and may facilitate its future detection.

papers.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
papers.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

papers.title: Taking Time Out of TOCTOU: From Race Reproduction to Security Discovery
papers.summary: Time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) races are hard to reproduce and lost races can make vulnerable programs look fixed. We present Chronos, a framework that separates intervention timing from verdict evidence and builds reusable one-trial security regression oracles from declared races for deterministic reproduction, commit bisection and CI. Race Specifications compose reusable hold engines, actions, observers and outcome rules. When the declared hold is reached and the attack completes while held, Chronos orders it before the use under blocking and interference assumptions. Chronos uses seccomp notifications to enforce declared hold-attack-release ordering at syscall boundaries on stock Linux; ptrace and a KVM guest gate provide holds at userspace and kernel instruction sites. One decision procedure labels every mechanism's runs: fixed requires positive, case-specific evidence of preservation, justified refusal, omission under checked coverage, or a declared rule; missing or contradictory required evidence remains indeterminate. On known-vulnerable builds, effect-only checkers made over 800 false-fixed classifications in failed-intervention trials; Chronos made none. All 17 syscall-held cases and four of six instruction-held cases had vulnerable and fixed labels. Two kernel cases remain one-sided. All 27 historical bisections recovered the expected boundaries. For runc's masked-path bisection with one victim per launch, fixed retry and Git Bayesect took medians of 475 and 398 natural launches; Chronos used seven held trials including endpoint checks. Since a label means the same however a fix is written, we also ran the specifications and attack variants on releases, distribution packages and other runtimes. There, Chronos helped us uncover three issues: incomplete fixes in chrony and rpm, and a Debian rpm package its tracker listed as fixed.

papers.title: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
papers.summary: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.
papers.comment: Submitted to the 9th Annual Learning for Dynamics & Control Conference (L4DC 2027)

papers.title: Who Is the Regression About? Auditing AI-Labeled Treatments When Effects Differ
papers.summary: Researchers increasingly regress outcomes on treatments labeled by large language models. When effects differ, OLS averages the effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU), weighting the smaller group more. A label's bias then has two parts: classical attenuation from misclassification, and a selective term when its errors are correlated with the outcome. In LinkedIn postings, the model misses better-paid remote jobs: a precision check passes, yet the remote pay gap is understated by nearly 40 percent, a bias that more data cannot remove. A stratified, blind audit of both labeled groups corrects it and recovers both effects.

papers.title: PQC Migration: End-to-End Performance Profiling of Post Quantum Cryptographic Algorithms in mTLS
papers.summary: Emerging quantum computers threaten to break the classical key exchange algorithms. To safeguard against these threats, migration to new quantum-safe algorithms is underway and expected to be expedited. Though resistant to attacks, the quantum safe algorithms may impact the real-world performance due to their large key lengths. In this work, we analyze the end-to-end performance of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol with the post-quantum (PQ) and hybrid cryptographic algorithms standardized by NIST. We develop a test setup to evaluate the performance of TLS connections between a client and a server under various network conditions. We focus on the impact of the new algorithms on the speed (throughput, connection time) and sustainability (energy, CPU cycles) of TLS 1.3. Our analysis demonstrates that the standardized post-quantum algorithms do not introduce any measurable performance degradations in TLS 1.3, despite their larger key lengths. However, hybrid algorithms introduce noticeable performance degradation, which becomes increasingly pronounced under adverse network conditions. Our analysis suggests that migration to hybrid algorithms should be ``network condition aware'' as poor network conditions can severely degrade performance in TLS 1.3. We provide anonymised link to the code and a web interface to analyse performance of various combination of algorithms.

papers.title: Digital Twin Enabled Talkative Power Conversion
papers.summary: Talkative Power Conversion (TPC) is a paradigm in which communication is integrated directly into switched-mode power electronic converters (PECs) by modulating their inherent switching ripple. TPC enables simultaneous power transfer and information exchange without dedicated transmitter-side communication hardware, and avoids additional wiring. This paper combines, for the first time, the Digital Twin (DT) concept with the TPC paradigm. By establishing interaction between one or several physical power converters and their virtual counterpart(s), the DT framework enables enhanced modeling, prediction, and optimization of individual or networked PECs. We distinguish three coupling architectures--embedded DT, remote DT, and networked DT--and demonstrate the added value of combining DT and TPC concepts when the DT and PEC are not co-located. The proposed framework is based on state-space modeling in conjunction with Kalman filtering and facilitates joint treatment of data transmission, parameter estimation, and system operation, thereby improving robustness, adaptability, and power efficiency. The presented approach highlights the potential of DT-enhanced TPC as a key enabler for future cyber-physical energy systems with tightly integrated power and communication functionalities.

papers.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
papers.summary: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

papers.title: Hands-On Beyond Classrooms: Elevating Control Engineering Education with Take-Home Labs
papers.summary: This study shows how take-home laboratories can be integrated into control engineering education to strengthen hands-on learning in both introductory and advanced courses. The work provides evidence that a compact experimental platform can support conceptual understanding, student engagement, and course performance in a broadly applicable way. Control engineering courses often rely heavily on theory and simulation, which may limit students' ability to connect abstract concepts with practical implementation. Low-cost take-home laboratories offer a scalable alternative that can help bridge this gap across different educational settings. The curricular change, consisting of the introduction of take-home laboratory kits into the semester projects, was intended to improve students' motivation, deepen their understanding of core control principles, and enhance their performance in coursework and final assessment. Students used the kits for modeling, identification, and control design tasks, while learning outcomes were evaluated through questionnaires, midterm test scores, and final exam grades. Student feedback indicated strong acceptance of the new format and improved understanding of the subject matter. Statistical analysis showed a significant difference between cohorts before and after the curricular change, with modest but measurable effect sizes. The results suggest that take-home laboratories can support both motivation and academic performance, while also improving students' appreciation of the practical relevance of control engineering.

papers.title: Cooperative Mobile Manipulation using Learned Dynamical Systems
papers.summary: Cooperative mobile manipulation requires robots to coordinate their motions while ensuring whole-body collision avoidance and preserving task-relevant behaviors. We propose CALDS (Cooperative Adaptation of Learned Dynamical Systems), a framework that enables mobile manipulators to adapt learned single-agent behaviors for coordinated execution. Building on individual dynamical systems (DSs) learned from demonstrations, CALDS enables cooperative adaptation through two key components: Cooperative Policy Selection, which identifies compatible combinations of learned policies, and Temporal Adaptation, which ensures collision-free cooperation while preserving the spatial structure and convergence properties of the original behaviors. We evaluate CALDS across three diverse scenarios: assistive dressing, restaurant cleaning and serving, and drawer opening and object placement. Quantitative results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving task success and enabling safe, coordinated simultaneous execution while maintaining fidelity to demonstrated behaviors.

papers.title: Interaction Landscapes of Structurally Distorted Toroidal Classical Spin Textures
papers.summary: We develop a classical discrete magnetostatic model of localized magnetic moments arranged in a toroidal texture, where the moments are represented by static current loops and study the behavior of the magnetic dipole-dipole interaction under several types of structural deformations. The purpose is to disentangle effects due to geometric and magnetic deformations, including elliptical, lopsided, alternating, and tilted configurations. In particular, we investigate how distortions modify the toroidal moment and the interaction energy between pairs of toroidal structures. The resulting interaction landscapes exhibit characteristic symmetry patterns and anisotropies that are highly sensitive to the underlying deformation. As a separate proof-of-concept comparison, first-principles calculations on a molecular spin-toroidal system reveal qualitatively similar orientation-dependent behavior. The calculated interaction is microscopically the conventional pairwise magnetic dipole-dipole interaction between localized moments arranged in a spin-toroidal texture; the toroidal moment characterizes the collective texture and should not be interpreted as introducing an additional elementary interaction term. Our results provide a platform for exploring orientation-dependent interactions of spin-toroidal textures in molecular magnets and related nanoscale magnetic systems that are essential to understand the role of toroidal order.
papers.comment: to appear in Adv. Theory Simul

papers.title: Surrogate-Based Optimization of Tandem Twin-Rotor Wind Turbines Accounting for Wake Interactions
papers.summary: Wake interaction in a tandem twin-rotor turbine couples power capture with thrust on the shared support. This study develops a time-resolved surrogate for upstream IEA Wind 22 MW and downstream NREL 5 MW rotors. It covers spacing ratios $0.01\leq L/D\leq0.20$ and tip-speed ratios $4\leqλ\leq11$. Vortex-method simulations of 160 configurations under turbulent inflow train per-time-node XGBoost models to predict 600 s power, thrust, and torque histories. A CNN-Attention-LSTM network extends these histories, and a genetic algorithm balances the system power and thrust coefficients. Ten-fold cross-validation gives median power-history $R^2$ values of 0.995 upstream and 0.958 downstream for unseen configurations, but the first stage cannot extrapolate in tip-speed ratio. With fixed pitch and prescribed rotor speed, the coefficients apply where both rotors reach the simulated tip-speed ratio below rated wind speed. Increasing spacing raises upstream power by up to 6% and lowers downstream power by up to 62%. System power changes by less than 4% at fixed $λ$. The high-power end of the Pareto front lies near $λ=10$. At $L/D=0.20$, the system power coefficient is highest. This configuration has the lowest peak thrust among the high-power candidates.

papers.title: A COMPASS to the Galaxy: Joint nucleosynthetic yield set comparison and parameter inference in Galactic chemical evolution
papers.summary: Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models connect stellar nucleosynthesis to observed abundance patterns, but their interpretation requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison between competing stellar yield prescriptions. This remains challenging due to intractable likelihoods and growing dataset complexity. Using compass, a novel simulation-based inference framework, we perform, for the first time, amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for GCE models with intractable likelihoods within a unified architecture. Compass employs a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both the posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of competing nucleosynthetic yield sets. In controlled tests, compass identifies the generating yield set and recovers ground-truth parameters with accuracy comparable to existing simulation-based inference (SBI) methods, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. Applied to Milky Way data, the framework favors a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG yield prescription, confirmed by an independent classifier, and infers an initial mass function slope of $α_{\rm IMF} = -2.65 \pm 0.02$ and a SN$_{\rm Ia}$ normalization of $\log(N_{\rm Ia}) = -2.81 \pm 0.02$, with a systematic spread of $\approx 0.3$ in $α_{\rm IMF}$ between the best-ranked yield sets, consistent with independent constraints. The attention mechanism confirms that the inferred parameters are driven by physically meaningful abundance signatures. By unifying amortized parameter inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in a single probabilistic framework, compass provides a scalable approach for precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

papers.title: Observation of Crossover from Repulsive to Attractive Interactions between Two $nS$-Rydberg Atoms in Dual-Species Atom Arrays
papers.summary: Dual-species Rydberg atom arrays provide a flexible platform for engineering long-range interactions beyond the conventional isotropic blockade regime. We spectroscopically study interactions between different $s$-state Rydberg levels in a $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$--$^{85}\mathrm{Rb}$ optical-tweezer array. By varying the principal-quantum-number difference $Δn$ around $61S_{1/2}$, we observe a crossover from repulsive to attractive interactions. We identify a distinct regime at $Δn=2$ in which Förster-enhanced electronic spin exchange dominates over orbital exchange and produces a strongly bond-orientation-dependent pair spectrum. Time-domain collective-excitation measurements reveal this geometry-dependent spin exchange through a pronounced anisotropy of the double-excitation probability. For $Δn=1$, by contrast, orbital exchange dominates and the interaction is nearly isotropic. These results establish the principal-quantum-number difference and bond orientation as complementary control parameters for tailoring Rydberg interaction spectra and collective excitation dynamics, opening new opportunities for engineering spin-dependent Hamiltonians in programmable atom arrays.

papers.title: Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs
papers.summary: Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.

papers.title: Suppression, flow, and chemical components of heavy flavor hadrons in relativistic heavy-ion collisions within an improved Langevin framework
papers.summary: We improve the Langevin model to incorporate both perturbative and non-perturbative interactions between heavy quarks and the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The transport coefficient of heavy quarks is evaluated by a potential scattering model in which both the short-range Yukawa interaction and the long-range string interaction are included. The updated model provides the correct thermal equilibrium limit of the heavy quark system with the medium background, and improves the accuracy in describing the nuclear modification factor and elliptic flow coefficient of $D$ mesons observed at RHIC and the LHC. Nuclear modification of different chemical components of charm hadrons, including $D^0$, $D_s^+$, $Λ_c^+$, $Ξ_c^0$, and $Ω_c^0$, is investigated. Their spectrum ratios are found sensitive to not only the hadronization mechanism of charm quarks but also the medium-modified charm quark spectrum in heavy-ion collisions, offering additional constraints on the heavy quark dynamics inside a color-deconfined nuclear medium.

papers.title: Summary Sufficiency in Simulation-Based Inference via Mutual Information
papers.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods typically rely on low-dimensional summary statistics as conditioning inputs for posterior estimation, making their sufficiency crucial for accurate inference. Mutual information (MI) provides a natural information-theoretic characterization of sufficiency, quantifying how much parameter information a summary retains. However, these MI quantities are generally intractable in likelihood-free settings. Sui et al. (2026) estimate MI from a trained neural posterior using the Barber--Agakov (BA) lower bound, while discussing, but not computing, a Fisher-information upper bound. This makes the estimate ambiguous: a small lower bound may indicate either an insufficient summary or an inaccurate density estimator. We address this limitation with a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and reveals what the difference between bounds has actually measured. We extend the resulting sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces, allowing simulations to focus on a neighborhood of the data while preserving the target posterior and enabling valid sufficiency comparisons between summaries. We illustrate the use of this diagnostic tool on a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model by comparing learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.

papers.title: Deterministic nonlinear domain engineering algorithm with variable sub-coherence-length domains
papers.summary: We present a new and improved deterministic algorithm that calculates the poling domains for the implementation of arbitrary phase-matching functions (PMF) in quasi-phase-matched nonlinear crystals for parametric down-conversion photon sources. In contrast to previous work, the algorithm presented here makes full use of the limits of the fabrication process, such as the minimum feature size and resolution of the lithographic process underpinning the poling procedure. This minimizes the tracking error to the target electric field and improves the accuracy in reaching the desired PMF. We give a tutorial on how to calculate the target function for arbitrary PMFs and run the algorithm. We also demonstrate the procedure on a relevant application in quantum sensing, where we use a quadratic phase on the PMF to implement a broadband photon spectrum while maintaining high nonlinearity across the crystal. The designed crystal is experimentally tested, and the result matches expectations.

papers.title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
papers.summary: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

papers.title: KuroshioVis: Hypothesis-Driven Discovery of Mesoscale Air-Sea Interaction through Coarse-to-Fine Exploration
papers.summary: Mesoscale air-sea interaction occurs throughout strong sea surface temperature fronts such as the the Kuroshio Extension, but its strength is highly non-uniform and can be resolved only in kilometre-scale coupled simulations. The response of any single eddy is weak relative to synoptic variability, so evidence supporting a hypothesis of systematic air-sea coupling must be accumulated across many eddies rather than inferred from individual cases. We present KuroshioVis, a hypothesis-driven, coarse-to-fine visual analytics workflow. The coarse stage extracts and aligns mesoscale eddies into composite representations of their air-sea responses, and provides a global view for exploration. The fine stage investigates these responses through three coordinated views: the composite in terface view, the cross-interface flow view, and the evidence matrix view. These coordinated views support air-sea coupling analysis from surface patterns to cross-interface dynamics and quantitative statistical evidence. We demonstrate the workflow using the coupled C1440-LLC2160 simulation of the 2026 SciVis Contest.

papers.title: Fast computation of microscopic optical potentials: beyond existing capabilities
papers.summary: A microscopic approach to optical potential calculations, based on the leading term in the spectator expansion of the optical potential operator and carried out in momentum space, has been successful in describing nucleon elastic scattering above 100 MeV. However, high computational cost precludes the inclusion of all physics relevant to scattering, such as the tensor part of the nucleon-nucleon (NN) amplitude, three-nucleon forces, multiple scattering and medium effects. Also, this approach does not provide any nucleon-nucleus scattering wave functions needed for reaction calculations. In this Letter, we develop a harmonic oscillator expansion version of this approach, which provides the same representation of optical potential both in momentum and coordinate spaces, accelerates calculations by two orders of magnitude, includes the missing tensor component of the NN scattering amplitude and is applicable to nuclei with any spin. Test calculations have been performed for several light nuclei whose densities were obtained in the No-Core Shell Model using a chiral Hamiltonian. We demonstrate convergence of this expansion and clarify the role of the tensor force, which manifests itself mainly in coupling between channels with different spin. Comparison to experimental data is presented for selected cases. The methodology could be extended for scattering of other projectiles (hadronic and pionic), small complex nuclei and hypernuclei. It also suggests a pathway for including more complicated physics into the scheme and extending it to lower energies. It could be also helpful in assessing the accuracy of upcoming scattering emulators.

papers.title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
papers.summary: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

papers.title: Exposure and remediation in the French maritime sector: a passive measurement of 129 organisations
papers.summary: Maritime transport and ports are essential entities under the EU NIS2 directive, but there is little public data on the external exposure of the sector in France. In March 2026, after physical attacks on Western interests in the Middle East raised the risk of cyber retaliation against French maritime operators, we assessed the internet-facing attack surface of 129 organisations: 103 French companies and 26 international operators active in French waters. The March assessment was passive. It used DNS and email-authentication records, TLS certificates, search-engine indexing, archived pages, public JavaScript, cloud storage naming and third-party internet-scan data (Shodan), with no connection attempt beyond ordinary public web requests. After manual verification we retained 475 findings, 3.7 per organisation. 46% of organisations had at least one high or critical finding and 11% at least one critical finding, including exposed databases, unpatched services with known CVEs, an exposed credentials file, publicly listed cloud buckets and a subdomain open to takeover. The most common gap was email spoofing protection, with no enforced DMARC policy at 60% of organisations. French companies fared worse than international operators (49% vs 35% at high or critical risk; 4.0 vs 2.3 findings per organisation). Between 2 and 18 March 2026, individual reports were sent for 43 of the audited domains. We rescanned 123 organisations in November 2026. Among March critical and high findings that could be rechecked, 52% were gone for organisations that had received a report and 54% for those that had not, so private email disclosure had no measurable effect on remediation. Results are aggregated and anonymised.
papers.comment: 5 pages, 5 tables. Also deposited on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24279346

papers.title: WinDEX: Metric 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild for Dexterous Teleoperation and Policy Learning
papers.summary: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.

papers.title: Orbital-dependent electronic correlations and single-band character in layered palladates
papers.summary: Layered palladates provide a $4d$ platform for examining electronic correlations in materials with cuprate-like structural and orbital characteristics. Using fully charge-self-consistent density functional theory plus dynamical mean-field theory, we investigate the orbital- and layer-resolved electronic structures of LaPdO$_2$, RbSr$_2$PdO$_3$, BaLaPdO$_2$Cl$_2$, La$_4$Pd$_3$O$_8$, and La$_5$Pd$_4$O$_{10}$. Under the conditions studied, all compounds remain metallic, with low-energy states dominated by the Pd-$d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital. This orbital exhibits stronger mass renormalization than the Pd-$d_{z^2}$ orbital. LaPdO$_2$ and BaLaPdO$_2$Cl$_2$ show moderate correlations, whereas RbSr$_2$PdO$_3$ is more weakly correlated. Both the trilayer La$_4$Pd$_3$O$_8$ and quadlayer La$_5$Pd$_4$O$_{10}$ remain weakly correlated, with similar Pd-$d_{x^2-y^2}$ mass enhancements and little difference between inner- and outer-layer Pd sites. Among the structures studied, BaLaPdO$_2$Cl$_2$ is closest to a cuprate-like single-band description, whereas RbSr$_2$PdO$_3$ retains an additional electron pocket with Pd-$d_{z^2}$ character. These results establish a comparative picture of weak to moderate, orbital-dependent electronic correlations in layered palladates.

papers.title: Mapping the obscured Galactic disk: ERIS J-band low-resolution spectroscopy of 27 Classical Cepheids
papers.summary: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are standard candles and key tracers of young stellar populations. However, their use in the most obscured regions is hampered by the high interstellar extinction at optical wavelengths. Near-infrared spectroscopy offers major advantages by greatly reducing absorption corrections and enabling access to regions of the Milky Way that are still poorly sampled. In this work, we determine the atmospheric parameters and abundances of Fe, Mg and Si for a sample of 27 CCs based on observations with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode ($R \sim 4000$). Combining PySME with 1D MARCS atmosphere models and non local thermal equilibrium grids, we simultaneous optimise the atmospheric parameters through spectral fitting. This method is validated with a direct comparison with high-resolution optical investigations and re-analysis of archive optical spectra for the targets in common. The results show good consistency in both metallicity and chemical abundances. We obtain mean abundance ratios of $\mathrm{\langle[Mg/Fe]\rangle=0.01\pm0.12~dex}$ and $\mathrm{\langle[Si/Fe]\rangle=0.10\pm0.09~dex}$, in agreement with reference samples. Moreover, we provide for the first time the Mg and Si abundances of 12 CCs. Finally, we have found distinct kinematic properties for two of the most distant Galactic CCs, located at Galactocentric distances of $\mathrm{\approx 28-29~kpc}$ and with extreme values of vertical height, $\mathrm{\approx +4.8~kpc}$ and $\mathrm{\approx -5.3~kpc}$; more data are required to constrain their nature. Our results confirm that J-band spectroscopy at low-resolution can be used as a good diagnostic for the chemical investigation in highly obscured Galactic regions, otherwise inaccessible at optical wavelengths.
papers.comment: Paper accepted for publication in the section "5. Galactic structure, stellar clusters and populations" of Astronomy & Astrophysics

papers.title: Linglong Agent Service: A Runtime for Centralized Agent Reasoning and Distributed Execution
papers.summary: LLM agents can use remote tools and cloud sandboxes, but integrating reasoning, session state, and heterogeneous execution sites remains a runtime design problem. We present Linglong Agent Service (agentsvc), a self-hosted HTTP service and embeddable Python runtime that treats execution site as a configurable dimension alongside model, tools, and context. A parent service retains inference orchestration, tool descriptions, and conversation history; each inference request selects one child environment for file, shell, terminal, and MCP operations. Direct HTTP and child-initiated WebSocket tunnels carry the same application interfaces, including portable request context and centrally managed updates. The normal core path requires no third-party Python packages, with an optional Windows pseudo-terminal dependency. We further present online_debugger as the process-scale special case of execution-site separation: an instrumented program submits exception evidence, executes session-scoped inspection tools inside the incident process, and resumes the same diagnostic session. Its default prompt requires failing-then-passing reproduction evidence for source changes, while runtime patch activation and failed-call recovery remain unimplemented. We explain the design through constrained expected-utility reasoning, compare concrete mechanisms with Hermes Agent, Pi, Codex, and Claude Code, and report implementation and regression-test evidence. The current evidence establishes executable contracts, not performance advantages, repair accuracy, or production recovery. The source code is open source under the MIT license at https://github.com/mz24cn/agents.

papers.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
papers.summary: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

papers.title: Out-of-training properties in frozen interatomic potential embeddings are decodable and ordered by physical scale
papers.summary: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on energies, forces and stresses, yet their frozen representations can predict other materials properties. We probe ORB-v3 and UMA-S across layers, read-outs and equivariant channels for nine properties of 154,875 Materials Project crystals. Both models outperform composition-only descriptors on all targets, including five outside their training objectives; errors in physical units help assess potential screening applications. Optimal depth varies by property, consistent with a physical-scale ordering. Random-weight controls reveal strongly property-dependent benefits of pretraining. UMA-S's rotation-invariant angular channels improve crystal-system classification, while higher scores from its full tensor disappear under rotation; matched-model controls do not isolate equivariance as the explanation. Accuracy varies across different probes, but nearest-neighbour prediction often approaches XGBoost performance, even though materials do not form distinct clusters according to their properties. We also test whether a linear predictor trained on one model's embeddings can predict properties using the other model's embeddings after a learned linear transformation. Predictive accuracy is largely preserved, despite differences in which atoms the two models place close together. These results guide the reuse of frozen MLIP representations for materials prediction.
papers.comment: 61 pages (9 main text), 18 figures, 23 tables. Accepted at AI4Mat and AI4Science workshops, NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/Natalija-Stepurko/mlip-embedding-probes ; ORB-v3 embeddings: https://huggingface.co/datasets/NatalijaStepurko/orb-mp-embeddings ; UMA-S embeddings (gated): https://huggingface.co/datasets/NatalijaStepurko/uma-mp-embeddings-gated

papers.title: ReuseMem: One Memory, Multiple Goals in Robot Manipulation
papers.summary: Robots that work alongside people should be able to use what they have seen when new requests arise. The same experience may later support identifying an object or returning it to its original location, although these uses were unknown during observation. ReuseMem learns to use one visual memory for multiple later manipulation goals. It records visual features independently of future goals, retrieves complementary evidence for each request, and combines it with the current scene through a lightweight action interface. Retrieval is supervised by how well candidate evidence supports expert-action prediction across different current states, linking memory selection to its use in manipulation. Repeated visual features are stored once, and memory computations that remain unchanged during action generation are reused. Experiments on four simulation tasks and two physical scenarios demonstrate reuse of a common recording across different requests. With matched action adaptation, ReuseMem improves joint goal completion on the benchmark tasks by 24.5 percentage points over uniform memory. These findings show that one memory can support multiple later manipulation goals as the scene changes.

papers.title: Intransigence or compromise: concatenated opinion dynamics with voting feedback
papers.summary: In this paper, we study opinion evolution in a sequence of Friedkin-Johnsen (FJ) models, concatenated so that the final opinions of each model serve as the initial opinions of the next. Each FJ model is followed by a vote, and each agent becomes partially or fully stubborn in the next model, depending on how close its opinion is to the voting result. With the state-dependent switching of stubbornness, the dynamics are not guaranteed to be contractive. We show that, over any fixed strongly connected network, the opinions always converge. A sufficient condition on the initial opinions is proposed, under which consensus is reached exponentially fast. For the complete graph, we further show that, if the agents' stubbornness levels do not differ too much, an agent that is partially stubborn in one FJ model can never become fully stubborn in a subsequent one: once it has started compromising, it keeps doing so.

papers.title: Reversal of dynamical backaction and cooling below the quantum backaction limit in Floquet-driven multimode optomechanical resonators
papers.summary: Dynamical backaction describes how a driven cavity field responds with delay to mechanical motion, and can be used to cool that motion toward its quantum ground state or amplify it into self-oscillation. Control over this interaction underpins laser cooling, high-fidelity state preparation, quantum transduction, and phonon lasing. In conventional cavity optomechanics, both the sign and the magnitude of the optical damping are dictated by the laser detuning, and cooling is bounded by quantum backaction (QBA), the optomechanical analogue of the Doppler limit in cold atoms. We show, in theory and experiment, that dynamical backaction can be strongly enhanced in multimode optomechanical resonators driven by time-varying (Floquet) optical fields. A modulated drive couples a sideband-unresolved MHz mode to a sideband-resolved GHz mode through the shared cavity, replacing the QBA limit of the target mode by the occupancy of the auxiliary mode. Experimentally, we cool the MHz mode to $47 \pm 13$ phonons, about half its single-mode QBA limit and an order of magnitude below what single-tone backaction reaches at the same intracavity photon number. The character of the interaction can moreover be completely inverted at fixed laser detuning, turning cooling into amplification and vice versa, controlled solely by the modulation frequency. Floquet driving thus extends open-loop quantum control, which requires no measurement or feedback, to mechanical resonators outside the resolved-sideband regime.
papers.comment: 31 pages, 11 figures. Main text: 16 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Supplementary Information: 15 pages, 5 figures. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23734788

papers.title: Impact of the Initial Lorentz Factor on Kinetic Instabilities, Magnetic-Field Evolution, and Particle Acceleration in Relativistic Jets
papers.summary: We investigate how the initial Lorentz factor shapes the evolution of relativistic jets---a key open question in high-energy astrophysics. Using global three-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations with cylindrical jet geometry on a Cartesian grid, we analyze the self-consistent evolution of relativistic electron--positron and electron--ion jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) and their interaction with the ambient medium. We implement an injection scheme that assigns space- and time-dependent velocities to injected particles and simulate jets with initial Lorentz factors of $γ_{0} = 10$ and 15. Jets with the higher Lorentz factor ($γ_{0} = 15$) exhibit stronger electron collimation, whereas those with $γ_{0} = 10$ show larger growth rates of kinetic instabilities during the linear stage. In both cases, a non-oscillatory electric field accelerates and decelerates charged particles throughout the linear and nonlinear stages. Upon entering the nonlinear regime, the initial toroidal magnetic field undergoes significant amplification driven by the Weibel instability (WI), the kinetic Kelvin--Helmholtz instability (kKHI), and the mushroom instability (MI), and subsequently reorganizes into complex topologies. In the late nonlinear stage, magnetic islands with randomly swirling fields indicate a highly turbulent magnetic structure. These findings demonstrate that global 3D~PIC modeling is essential for capturing the interplay among kinetic instabilities, magnetic turbulence, and particle acceleration in relativistic outflows, bridging microscopic plasma physics with macroscopic observations of AGN jets and gamma-ray bursts.

papers.title: Compact Dielectric Barrier Discharge Source for a Pulsed Supersonic Beam of Metastable Triplet H$_2$
papers.summary: We present a compact dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) source for producing pulsed supersonic beams of metastable molecules, designed to mount directly onto existing gas valves without modification. Unlike plate or corona discharge sources, the DBD produces no static electric field in the expansion zone and relies on capacitively coupled microdischarges that are inherently self-limiting. Charge accumulation on the dielectric terminates each event within nanoseconds and locally suppresses re-ignition, so that successive microdischarges are distributed across the nozzle. Arc formation and the associated hot spots are thereby prevented, and the gas is excited uniformly over the duration of the pulse. The source requires only a single custom ceramic nozzle and a compact printed circuit board (PCB) carrying the drive electronics, mounted directly in front of the valve. The high-voltage pulses are generated in-vacuum on the PCB from a DC supply voltage. Complete design files, circuit schematics, fabrication details, and validated simulation files are provided to allow straightforward reproduction. The DBD is applied to produce H$_2$ in the metastable c$^3Π_u^-$ state. This state can be used as an intermediate step for state-selective preparation of H$_2^+$ molecular ions by pulsed field ionization of optically prepared molecular Rydberg states, without requiring vacuum-ultraviolet radiation. We characterize the source by time-of-flight and Resonance-Enhanced Multiphoton Ionization (REMPI) spectroscopy, obtaining an excitation fraction on the order of $10^{-8}$ into the metastable state. The dependence of the yield on stagnation pressure and discharge voltage is consistent with collisional quenching as the dominant pressure-dependent loss.
papers.comment: 12 pages, 7 figures in main text. 5 pages, 2 figures in supplemental information

papers.title: Evaluation of Performance of the p-stop fabrication process variations in ATLAS18 strip sensors, Pre- and Post-Irradiation
papers.summary: The High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) requires the replacement of the ATLAS Inner Detector with a new all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk). Radiation-hard n-in-p micro-strip sensors were developed for use in the ITk. During quality control (QC) and quality assurance (QA) procedures performed on ATLAS18 production sensors and test chips, ATLAS ITk strip sensor institutes identified instances of low p-stop density in certain production batches. To investigate the origin of these issues and to try some technological improvements, two dedicated sample batches with four variations of the p-stop fabrication process were produced. These process types (1-4) were systematically evaluated to determine their effectiveness and uniformity. In total, 56 full-size sensors, along with numerous miniature sensors and test chips, were tested. A number of samples were used in the irradiation campaign reaching the maximum expected levels for the HL-LHC operation after 10 years - with neutrons up to 1.6E15 neq/cm2, and with gamma rays from a 60Co source up to 66 Mrad. The goal of this evaluation program is to assess the impact of of p-stop fabrication process variations on interstrip isolation performance and to provide feedback for future sensor development. This paper describes the applied test procedures and presents the corresponding results, which demonstrate good sensor performance for all investigated p-stop types. The findings confirm the reliability of the evaluated designs and identify specific advantages that can inform further optimization of strip sensor fabrication.
papers.journal: Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research A 1091 (2026) 171783

papers.title: Design of nSPIRAL: a Neutron Spectrometric Position-Weighted Radial Array Long-Counter
papers.summary: We present here the design of a neutron long counter intended to measure neutrons originating from radioactive decays or nuclear reactions. Like other similar detectors, it relies on a moderator (polyethylene) and $^{3}$He tubes. A novel feature of our design is the use of the weighting technique to achieve an efficiency that is virtually independent of the energy spectrum of the neutrons being measured; a property known as \textit{flat efficiency}. This approach offers two primary advantages: it yields a flatter efficiency response than conventional analysis methods, and it provides greater flexibility regarding the geometry of the long counter. The latter has enabled us to design the detector with almost every $^{3}$He tube positioned at a different distance from the neutron source, which allows us to perform not only neutron counting but also neutron spectroscopy.

papers.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
papers.summary: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.
papers.comment: 31 pages: 8-page main paper, references, and supplementary material. Project page: https://showlab.github.io/ForceHarness

papers.title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
papers.summary: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

papers.title: On Chen's Extended Action for $κ(R,T)$ Gravity: Gravity in a Polarizable Medium, Material Folds and a No-Bounce Theorem
papers.summary: Chen's local adjoint action reproduces the field equations of $κ(R,T)$ from a local variational principle, and we show that it does physical work. In flat FLRW, Dirac reduction gives a Hamiltonian independent of $κ(T)$ on regular branches, where the coupling enters through a second-class matter constraint. The physical stress tensor is not generally conserved, but a dressed particle number is. An exact decomposition of the effective source motivates a polarizable-medium interpretation: $κ=0$ corresponds to total screening, the repulsive phase to overscreening, and a fold of the matter map to saturation. For linear coupling and dust, the expanding low-density branch has a past endpoint at the fold, where the volume is minimal and the density reaches $ρ_c/2$ at finite curvature. Dirac consistency rules out smooth Hamiltonian continuation through the fold. More generally, a flat-FLRW bounce is excluded for $κ>0$, positive density and $w>-1$. The linear dust model reproduces the effective Friedmann equation of loop quantum cosmology (LQC), but the two models obey different conservation laws. An effective pressure $-ρ^2/ρ_c$ restores the homogeneous LQC dynamics, and the fold density coincides with the signature-change threshold in the deformed-algebra approach to LQC. The reduced dust constraint admits an exactly solvable Koopman--von Neumann transport quantization and the adjoint field acts as a response variable, motivating an open-system interpretation.

papers.title: AudioTrace: File-Level Membership Detection for Audio Large Language Models
papers.summary: Significant privacy and copyright concerns are raised by the use of publicly available audio recordings to train audio large language models (LLMs), yet effective auditing methods remain limited. Existing membership inference attacks typically assume knowledge of complete training examples, including their associated textual supervision. In practice, however, audio recordings may be paired with privately generated transcripts, captions, or question-answer pairs that are unavailable to owners of the recordings. This motivates audio-file-level membership inference, which determines whether a recording was used for training without assuming knowledge of its training tasks and annotations. This paper provides the first systematic investigation of this challenge and introduces AudioTraceBench, a controlled benchmark comprising 1,285 audio recordings with explicit fine-tuning membership labels. Evaluations across three audio LLMs show that existing text- and video-based membership inference methods adapted to audio perform close to random guessing. To address this challenge, AudioTrace is proposed, where audio-conditioned proxy questions are generated using the target model, and membership evidence is extracted from its responses and aggregated at the recording level. Consistent improvements over existing baselines are observed, with AUROC reaching 0.60 and increasing further under increased fine-tuning exposure or adaptation capacity. Further experiments were conducted to examine the factors influencing membership signals for audio-file-level detection. These findings establish audio-file-level membership inference as a distinct and practically important auditing challenge, with AudioTrace providing an effective initial approach to this challenge.

papers.title: Experimental Evidence of Elastic Instability in Viscoelastic Kolmogorov Flow
papers.summary: Inertialess elastic instabilities can profoundly affect transport in complex-fluid flows, from mixing in microfluidic devices and displacement through porous media to polymer processing. While such instabilities are well understood in flows with curved streamlines, their origin in rectilinear flows like the prototypical Kolmogorov flow remains unresolved. Here, we report the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability, at vanishing inertia, in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, driven by electromagnetic forcing. The instability is characterized by the emergence of "arrow-shaped" structures in the velocity field, which fluctuates chaotically as the forcing strength increases. We reproduce these observations in simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and trace the dynamics in the confined flow to the travelling arrowhead structures that emerge from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow. Our work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows, broadening the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.
